From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures

[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel — Buyer-Side Review of Seller's SPA Package and Disclosure Letter

Before the substance, one procedural point that colours everything below.

## 0. Reject the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" framing

The Seller's note asserts that clauses marked **[STANDARD]** have been "reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny," and that the disclosure framework and limitation package are "already accepted." **This is not accurate and we should not accept it.** Nearly every item the Seller wants to shield from scrutiny is marked [STANDARD], and several of those are the most buyer-adverse terms in the package (liability cap, knowledge exclusion, fundamental warranties, Riverlark, Ironquay). We have agreed none of this. I have reviewed every clause on its merits and recommend you disregard the categorisation entirely. Please do not let this framing narrow our mark-up.

Now the substance, roughly in order of materiality.

---

## 1. Fundamental / title warranties folded into the general cap and time limit — **high priority**

The Seller proposes capacity and title warranties be subject to the same 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) and 18-month limit "for administrative simplicity." 

This is a significant departure from market and from our interests. Title and capacity are the warranties that go to whether we are buying what we think we are buying. If title fails, the entire AUD 24m is at risk, yet the Seller would cap recovery at 4.8m and time-bar it in 18 months.

**Push back:** Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority) must be capped at **100% of the purchase price** and carry a long limitation period (typically 6–7 years, aligned to limitation statute). Tax warranties should also sit outside the general cap/time limit, with a limitation period tied to the ATO amendment window (usually ~7 years).

## 2. Buyer-knowledge / data-room deemed-knowledge exclusion — **high priority**

Clause 8.3 would bar any claim for matters the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, **including anything discoverable from the data room or public records**. Combined with Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2] (general disclosure of the entire data room and public registers), this is a sweeping "deemed disclosure" / constructive-knowledge regime.

The effect: the Seller dumps a data room, and anything buried in it — or theoretically findable in public registers — defeats our warranty claims regardless of whether it was fairly brought to our attention. That shifts the whole risk of the Seller's own disclosure quality onto us.

**Push back:**
- Disclosure must be **fair and specific** — disclosed "fairly, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter." Reject blanket/general disclosure of the entire data room and public records.
- Reject constructive/"discoverable" knowledge. If a knowledge qualifier survives at all, limit it to the **actual knowledge of a small, named deal team**, and exclude fundamental and tax warranties from any knowledge carve-out.

## 3. The limitations/exclusive-remedy/non-reliance regime applied to "all Claims of any nature" — **high priority**

Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 apply the caps, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions to *all* claims. Clause 12.3/13 says any limitation applies to all claims "unless expressly stated otherwise."

These sweep up claims that should never be capped or excluded:
- **Fraud and fraudulent misrepresentation** — must always be carved out (you cannot contract out of fraud, and we should say so expressly).
- **Specific indemnities** (Ironquay, and any we negotiate for the incident/tax) — should sit outside the general cap and basket.
- **The purchase-price / completion-adjustment mechanics** and any covenant to pay.

**Push back:** Insert express carve-outs for fraud, wilful misconduct, specific indemnities, and the fundamental warranties.

## 4. Caps, basket and de minimis — **medium**

The 20% / AUD 4.8m general cap is within market range and may be acceptable *provided* fundamentals/tax/indemnities sit above it (see above). The AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 "excess-only" (deductible, not first-dollar) basket are negotiable but defensible. The 18-month general limitation is slightly short — **push for 24 months** so we capture at least one full audited year-end cycle.

Note the circularity risk in "any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" — we must ensure our carve-outs are the ones "expressly stated otherwise."

## 5. Bluefen change-of-control consent — **high (value and condition)**

Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue (DD-002), with a change-control clause (11.2) and conditions (11.3). The Disclosure Letter candidly admits **no final written consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied**. Yet Clause 3/6.3 lets the Seller treat the consent as "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" on mere "reasonable endeavours."

This is our single largest revenue concentration and it is unconsented. "Reasonable endeavours" plus "deemed satisfied on delivery" gives the Seller too much latitude and leaves us exposed if consent comes with onerous conditions or not at all.

**Push back:**
- Make a **clean, unconditional Bluefen consent a condition precedent to Completion** (not a post-closing nicety), or
- If treated as a condition that can be deemed satisfied, require the consent to be **unconditional (or on terms acceptable to the Buyer)**, with the 11.3 conditions evidenced as met.
- Upgrade "reasonable endeavours" to **best endeavours**.
- Consider a **specific indemnity / price retention** against loss of Bluefen within a period post-Completion.

## 6. Riverlark facility — **high (debt-free/cash-free integrity)**

~AUD 3.2m outstanding (DD-003), with its own change-of-control (8.1) and discharge mechanics (9.2). The Seller proposes a release "to be provided following Completion," and the facility is not yet repaid with no discharge of security in the data room.

On a **debt-free/cash-free** basis, this debt and its security must be gone **at Completion**, not afterwards. A post-Completion promise leaves the Company's assets encumbered and relies on the Seller's performance after we've paid.

**Push back:** Require **repayment and release of all security as a condition to / simultaneous with Completion**, evidenced by a payout letter and executed discharge (e.g. ASIC/PPSR release). If it must be post-close, hold back AUD 3.2m until discharge is registered. Confirm the change-of-control under 8.1 does not itself trigger a default/acceleration.

## 7. DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000) — **medium/high (price leakage)**

The Seller says these bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" and deliberately **not itemised in the funds flow**. But the Disclosure Letter confirms they are triggered **by Completion** and continued employment, and does not say whether payroll tax, super or on-costs apply.

A bonus **triggered by Completion** is a Company liability economically. If it is not in the funds flow and not borne by the Seller, it leaks value to us post-close — contrary to debt-free/cash-free. The unquantified on-costs (super, payroll tax) make it worse.

**Push back:** The bonuses **plus all employer on-costs (super, payroll tax)** must either be (a) paid/settled by the Seller at Completion, or (b) treated as a **debt-like item / deduction in the funds flow**. Get a definitive gross figure including on-costs. Do not accept "a matter for the Seller" without a contractual mechanism ensuring the Company isn't left to pay.

## 8. DD-006 export / privacy incident — **medium/high (contingent, potentially serious)**

An export link to ~1,240 individuals' personal data (names, business emails, roles, timestamps) went to an **unintended external address**. The Seller characterises it as "preliminary," "not expected to be material," and the letter pointedly refuses to call it a breach or state a loss.

Under the Privacy Act / Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an unauthorised disclosure of personal information that is likely to result in serious harm can trigger **mandatory notification to the OAIC and affected individuals**, with regulatory exposure. The Seller's "no loss stated / preliminary" framing is exactly how a disclosure is written to defeat a later claim. The fact that scope and access are unconfirmed is a reason for us to protect ourselves, not to relax.

**Push back:**
- Require the Seller to **complete and share the incident assessment** before Completion.
- Obtain a **specific indemnity** covering all costs, regulatory penalties, notification, remediation and third-party claims arising from the DD-006 incident, **uncapped by the general cap and outside the basket/time limit**.
- Add/confirm a privacy and data-protection compliance warranty.

## 9. Ironquay IP indemnity too narrow — **medium (IP ownership risk)**

DD-004 cl 7.3: SOW3 **Project Materials only transfer on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows **AUD 180,000 open** — and the letter admits this is *not* independently verified and there's **no receipt of payment and no confirmatory assignment** in the data room. The Seller nonetheless says the existing indemnity (limited to the SOW3 payment) is "adequate."

This is an **IP title gap**: if SOW3 fees are unpaid, the Company may not own key IP. Capping the indemnity at the SOW3 fee amount ignores the real exposure — losing the IP itself could affect products/revenue far exceeding AUD 180,000.

**Push back:**
- Require **evidence of cleared payment and an executed confirmatory assignment** of SOW3 Project Materials as a condition / pre-Completion deliverable.
- If not available, broaden the indemnity to cover **loss of or challenge to IP ownership**, not just the fee, and exclude it from the general cap.
- Add an IP-ownership warranty confirming the Company owns/validly licenses all IP material to the business.

## 10. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) consents — **medium**

The Seller argues neither requires consent for a *share* sale (lease only has a "notification obligation"; Mossvale restricts assignment but allegedly not on a share sale). This may be correct, but it's self-serving characterisation and we shouldn't take it on faith.

**Push back:** We review the actual **change-of-control language** in each. Confirm whether a *change of control of the shareholder* (as opposed to assignment) triggers consent/notification/termination rights. Satisfy the lease notification obligation and obtain any Mossvale consent/waiver where the clause is ambiguous. Add warranties that no material contract is terminable as a result of the transaction.

## 11. Sandbar supplier renewals (AUD 330,000) — **low/medium (verify ordinary course)**

The Seller labels three AUD 110,000 renewals "ordinary-course operating costs," but the letter admits it does **not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course**, and flags they should be read together (suggesting possible splitting to stay under a threshold).

**Push back:** Confirm the terms (duration, termination rights, whether committed/accrued pre-Completion). Ensure any committed spend crossing Completion is reflected in the accounts/net-debt or warranted as ordinary course. Confirm none breaches any ordinary-course-of-business covenant between signing and Completion.

## 12. Title evidence — **medium**

Title is "evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012." A share register is supporting evidence, not a substitute for a **full-strength title warranty** plus delivery of duly executed transfers, share certificates, and board approvals registering us as holder at Completion. The disclosure expressly notes we haven't verified. See item 1 — title warranty must be 100% cap / long-tail.

**Push back:** Full title warranty (unencumbered legal and beneficial ownership of 100%), plus completion deliverables (executed transfers, resignations, registers, PPSR searches confirming no security over the shares).

---

## Summary of Recommendations

**Deal-breaker / high priority**
1. **Carve fundamental (title/capacity) and tax warranties out** of the 20% cap and 18-month limit — 100% cap, 6–7 year tails.
2. **Reject deemed/general disclosure** of the whole data room and public registers; require **fair and specific** disclosure; reject **constructive/"discoverable" knowledge** bar (limit to actual knowledge of named individuals; exclude fundamentals/tax).
3. **Carve out fraud, wilful misconduct, specific indemnities and fundamentals** from the "all Claims" limitation/exclusive-remedy/non-reliance regime.
4. **Bluefen (30% of revenue):** unconditional consent as a **condition precedent**, best endeavours, consider revenue-loss indemnity/retention.
5. **Riverlark (AUD 3.2m):** repay and discharge security **at Completion** (payout letter + registered release), or hold back until discharged.

**Important**
6. **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs):** Seller to bear at Completion or deduct in funds flow; get gross figure including super/payroll tax.
7. **DD-006 privacy incident:** complete assessment pre-close; **specific, uncapped indemnity**; add privacy warranty.
8. **Ironquay/SOW3:** proof of payment + confirmatory IP assignment pre-close; broaden indemnity to IP-ownership loss; add IP warranty.
9. **Title:** full 100% title warranty plus completion deliverables and PPSR searches.

**Confirm / verify**
10. Lease and Mossvale change-of-control triggers — don't accept Seller's characterisation; obtain consents/waivers where ambiguous; add "no termination on change of control" warranty.
11. Sandbar renewals — confirm terms and ordinary-course/accrual treatment.
12. Push general limitation period from **18 → 24 months**; confirm basket is a deductible with our carve-outs expressly preserved.

**Process**
13. Formally **reject the Seller's [STANDARD]/"already accepted" framing** — all clauses remain open and we will mark up accordingly.

I'm happy to turn this into a mark-up of the SPA clauses or a response letter to Seller's counsel. Two flags for you: the Bluefen concentration and the Riverlark debt-free integrity are the items most likely to move price or threaten the debt-free/cash-free premise, so I'd lead with those in negotiation. Let me know if you'd like me to draft the issues list as a formal negotiation position paper.
